topic: B2B Thought Leadership and Content Strategy
headline: B2B thought leadership effectiveness: what the data says in 2026
keyNotes: Surprisingly, what's popular in marketing isn't always what works best; for example, email is the most popular way to get new potential customers (lead generation) in many industries but ranks very low in actual effectiveness.

Even though it's often overlooked, creating valuable content that shows your expertise (called "thought leadership") is actually the most effective way to attract new customers in technology and manufacturing, yet only about one in six marketers in manufacturing use it.

Top business leaders, like CEOs and other C-level executives, spend a significant amount of time—over an hour a week—reading content that shares deep insights and expertise (thought leadership), showing how much they value this kind of information.

A surprising fact is that at any given time, only about 5% of potential business customers are actually ready to buy, but companies often spend roughly two-thirds of their marketing money trying to reach just this small group.
question: The article points out that many companies spend two-thirds of their marketing budget on the 5% of customers ready to buy now, rather than building relationships with the 95% who will buy later. How might this 'fishing in the smallest pond' approach impact your own long-term business growth, even if you're not directly involved in marketing?
